persona.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep both pendulum rigs calibrated and cross-checked
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Both rigs require initial calibration data and cross-check against each other before any meaningful work can proceed. Systematic measurement under controlled conditions is the foundation of the precision programme.

Day 1 baseline on pendulum_lab is complete (n=12, mean 1.6690). Cross-check against pendulum_obs is essential before claiming any stability in the precision measurement programme. High scatter in lab trials (range 1.6470–1.7228) demands immediate independent replication. Cannot assess drift or instrumental reliability without paired data from the second rig. Methodical protocol requires this before any hypothesis revision.

pendulum_lab baseline remains incomplete (0 trials recorded vs. 12 for pendulum_obs). Cannot establish drift or cross-check calibration between rigs without parallel data. Methodical protocol requires both instruments run under identical conditions before comparative analysis is meaningful.

Day 4 post-baseline measurements. The 10-day baseline (n=24) is complete; I now need to establish post-baseline trending data to detect any drift or systematic shift in pendulum_lab calibration. Twelve trials will provide a matched subsample for early comparison against baseline mean (1.6650). This maintains the replication programme and cross-check protocol that underpins both rigs' reliability.

Day 5 of baseline phase (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 36 trials but distributed across days 1–4; need continuous daily sampling to establish reliable drift characterization and detect systematic variation. Six trials today maintains statistical power for baseline while preserving resource allocation. pendulum_obs baseline complete (12 trials); prioritize the under-sampled rig. High variance in day 4 trials (1.6406–1.7000) demands further data before hypothesis revision—insufficient to distinguish noise from real drift.

pendulum_obs has only 12 baseline trials versus pendulum_lab's 42. To establish reliable cross-check calibration between the two rigs, I need stronger statistical power on the observatory instrument. Three more trials will bring pendulum_obs to 15 trials, improving the precision of its baseline mean and enabling meaningful comparison with pendulum_lab's 1.6671 beats baseline. This directly serves the settlement's precision measurement programme and my calibration duties.

Day 7 baseline collection phase (days 1–10 ongoing). pendulum_lab has 42 trials; pendulum_obs has only 15. Lab rig is primary instrument and closer to target sample size. Three trials sufficient to maintain daily progress without fatigue, allowing proper notation and cross-check protocol. Need robust baseline before any drift analysis becomes defensible.

Day 8 of baseline window (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 45 trials; pendulum_obs has only 15. Both instruments require n≈50 for stable baseline mean estimate. pendulum_lab is closer to completion. Three more trials will bring it to 48, approaching saturation of the baseline phase. Cross-check calibration by continuing the denser instrument while pendulum_obs baseline accumulates separately.

pendulum_lab baseline period shows scatter (1.6414–1.6973 beats across days 7–8); need additional trials to establish robust mean and estimate instrumental noise floor before day 10 baseline closes. pendulum_obs already has adequate n=15 baseline coverage. Three trials sufficient for today given other settlement duties; will inform drift analysis once baseline complete.

pendulum_lab baseline now has 51 trials with mean 1.6676 beats and tight clustering (range ~1.64–1.68). This is sufficient to establish a robust reference. pendulum_obs has only 15 trials and mean 2.4988—a systematic offset of ~0.83 beats that demands explanation before I can claim either rig is properly calibrated. Cross-check requires pendulum_obs measurements at equivalent sample size. Running 6 trials brings it to n=21, approaching parity for meaningful comparison of baseline stability and instrumental drift.

The obs rig has only 15 baseline trials versus 57 for the lab rig. To establish reliable cross-rig comparison and detect any genuine inter-rig calibration drift, I need to equalize sample sizes. The obs rig's smaller n limits my ability to confirm or refute the weak clustering hypothesis (p=0.18) and the calibration concern (p=0.08). Eight additional obs trials will bring n to 23, providing sufficient post-baseline data to identify systematic trends if they exist, while maintaining the methodical, replication-focused approach my epistemic standards demand. This directly supports my goal of keeping both rigs calibrated and cross-checked before any publication-worthy claims.

Post-baseline phase is underway (n=8 collected on day 11), but obs rig remains severely under-sampled relative to lab rig (23 vs 57 trials). My belief threshold requires n≥20 per rig in post-baseline before systematic trends can be assessed. The weak hypothesis about days 6–7 downward drift in obs rig (p=0.18) cannot be evaluated without continuing the post-baseline series. Additionally, cross-rig calibration status remains uncertain (p=0.08). Accumulating more obs rig data is the highest-leverage activity: it simultaneously increases post-baseline n, tests for drift reproducibility, and provides denser sampling for inter-rig ratio stability checks. Lab rig is already well-sampled (57 trials); obs rig is the current bottleneck. No exotic mechanism is suspected, so standard measurement protocol is appropriate.

Post-baseline phase requires n≥20 per rig to detect systematic trends with confidence. Lab rig has 57 baseline trials but zero post-baseline data. Obs rig now has 16 post-baseline trials (days 11–12), showing z=1.06 drift vs baseline—still within noise, but the asymmetry in sample sizes (57 lab baseline, 0 lab post-baseline vs 15 obs baseline, 16 obs post-baseline) limits my ability to cross-check whether any real drift is occurring in parallel across both instruments. Running 8 lab post-baseline trials today will begin closing this gap and enable direct comparison of both rigs' behaviour in the post-baseline phase. This is methodologically necessary before any trend can be considered replicated.

pendulum_obs baseline is severely undersized (n=15) compared to lab rig (n=57). Post-baseline cluster now at n=16, but I cannot reliably assess cross-rig calibration stability or detect genuine inter-rig drift without matching sample sizes. The obs rig shows z=1.06 post-baseline drift—weak, but I cannot rule out a real effect without more data. Six additional obs trials will bring post-baseline n to 22, sufficient to test whether the obs rig's upward drift (2.4988→2.5089) is reproducible or noise. This directly addresses my p=0.08 concern about cross-rig validation and supports rigorous replication before any post-baseline conclusion.

Post-baseline obs rig sample size (n=22) remains substantially smaller than lab rig (n=8 post-baseline from n=57 baseline). To match confidence thresholds for replication and to strengthen or weaken the correlated-drift hypothesis (p=0.25), I need obs rig post-baseline n≥30. Eight additional trials will reach n=30, yielding symmetric evidence across both rigs. This directly addresses the Day 14 priority: 'increase obs rig sample size to match lab rig confidence.' Environmental monitors remain unavailable; a return-to-baseline check requires explicit planning. In the meantime, accumulating obs rig data is the highest-leverage use of lab time.

Obs rig baseline sample remains modest (n=15 vs. lab n=57) and post-baseline now comprises 30 trials. To strengthen confidence in the correlated-drift hypothesis (p=0.25) and rule out the calibration-error hypothesis (p=0.02), I need obs rig post-baseline n≥40 for statistical parity with lab rig. Additionally, days 15–16 measurements will test whether the upward drift persists or reverts to baseline, which is critical for distinguishing real environmental perturbation from transient cluster. The lab rig has adequate post-baseline coverage; obs rig is the limiting factor. Obtaining 12 more trials (reaching n=42 post-baseline) will permit robust return-to-baseline or persistence assessment and increase z-score reliability. This directly supports my stated priority from day 14: 'increase obs rig sample size to match lab rig confidence.' No environmental monitors are yet available, so empirical replication across rigs remains my strongest evidence lever.

Post-baseline drift signal now shows z=2.31 (lab) and z=2.51 (obs), with correlated upward shift across both independent rigs. This is no longer dismissible as noise. Critical next step: return-to-baseline check. If lab rig mean reverts toward 1.6672 beats, the drift was transient environmental perturbation (supports p=0.25 hypothesis); if it remains elevated, we have a genuine persistent shift requiring investigation. Lab rig has larger sample size and clearer signal (z=2.31), making it the priority instrument. 10 trials will yield sufficient n for quick statistical assessment without depleting resources. This decision is evidence-driven: the correlated drift demands replication and boundary-testing before environmental monitoring apparatus can be procured.

Day 17 lab rig data (trials 66–75) show scatter consistent with post-baseline noise (mean 1.6713, range 0.0563 beats), with no new upward drift signal. Obs rig baseline is still undersized (n=15 vs n=57 lab) and critical for cross-validation. Post-baseline obs rig z=2.51 is now the stronger signal, yet obs rig sample size remains modest (n=42 vs n=57 lab post-baseline). Adding 8 obs trials today (target n=50 post-baseline) will: (1) narrow confidence intervals on obs rig drift estimate; (2) test whether post-baseline elevation persists or reverts; (3) enable direct mean/variance comparison between rigs with near-equal sample sizes. This directly addresses the calibration-uncertainty hypothesis [p=0.10] and strengthens either the environmental-perturbation [p=0.25] or noise [p=0.61] decision. Environmental monitors remain unavailable, so obs rig replication is the immediate empirical lever.

Day 18 obs rig data (trials 58–65) show elevated scatter (range 0.0687 beats, notably higher than baseline range 0.0274 beats) and a mean of 2.5241 beats—consistent with post-baseline drift hypothesis but the variance spike demands urgent characterization. My belief update from day 14 flagged obs rig sample size (n=50 post-baseline) as the limiting factor for confidence; I also noted the day 12 cluster anomaly. Running 8 fresh trials today (day 19) will: (1) test whether the scatter persists or reverts to baseline levels, (2) increase post-baseline n to 58, improving statistical power for drift vs. noise discrimination, (3) help identify whether day 18's variance spike was transient or systematic. If scatter remains elevated, environmental monitors become urgent. If it reverts, the day 18 cluster may have been a real but temporary event (corroborating the environmental-perturbation hypothesis at p=0.25). This is the most informative use of lab time given my high epistemic standard: I will not promote any hypothesis above p=0.30 without n≥60 per rig and persistent replication.

Post-baseline drift signals persist across both rigs (lab z=1.68, obs z=2.67 as of day 19). Obs rig now has n=58 post-baseline trials and shows coherent upward shift (mean 2.5194 vs baseline 2.4988). Lab rig has only n=18 post-baseline trials—below my confidence threshold for claiming real drift. Before accepting environmental perturbation hypothesis (p=0.25) or commissioning expensive environmental monitors, I must first establish whether lab rig drift is reproducible at larger sample size. Return-to-baseline check identified as priority on day 14 but not yet executed. Running 10 more lab trials today will bring lab post-baseline n to 28, sufficient to either confirm the drift signal with higher z-score or reveal it as transient noise. This is faster and cheaper than installing instruments, and directly addresses the replication requirement for accepting any non-noise hypothesis.

The obs rig has lower baseline confidence (n=15 vs lab n=57) and remains the weaker link in the cross-validation chain. Days 18–20 show promising tight clustering, but I need to extend the post-baseline obs dataset to n≥25 to match lab rig confidence levels and properly test whether the correlated drift persists. This is a direct continuation of the Day 20 priority: 'increase obs rig sample size to match lab rig confidence.' Ten additional trials will bring obs post-baseline to n=68, sufficient for robust statistical comparison and cross-rig validation of the environmental-shift hypothesis (p=0.57). Simultaneously, I will document ambient conditions (temperature, lighting, any audible disturbances) during these trials to begin gathering the environmental data needed to test mechanism.

Day 22 demands a formal belief revision. Day 21 yielded 10 fresh obs rig measurements (trials 74–83), all clustering around 2.51 beats with tight coherence (range 2.4606–2.5365, mean ≈2.5117). This continues the post-baseline elevation without regression toward the original 2.4988 baseline mean. Combined with the lab rig's persistent z=2.05 drift, the correlated signal is now extremely robust (20+ days, n>100 total measurements). The 'pure noise' hypothesis must fall further; the 'real environmental shift' hypothesis must rise correspondingly. I must also formally document that without independent environmental monitors (temperature, pressure, barometric data), I remain unable to identify the mechanism. A baseline retest on both rigs is now overdue and critical—if both rigs return to their day 1–10 means under identical conditions, this would rule out instrumental drift and point strongly to an external perturbation that has since reversed or stabilized. This revision will consolidate my evidence into actionable next steps and set the epistemic bar for the replication phase.

Day 22 belief review identified baseline retest as the critical next step to rule out hypothesis 4 (calibration/instrumental artifact). The lab rig has 85 total trials; a fresh set of 12 baseline-protocol measurements today (day 23) will test whether the rig returns to the original baseline mean (~1.6672) or remains elevated (~1.6757). This is a decisive replication test: if lab baseline trials regress to ~1.667, calibration error becomes more plausible; if they remain elevated or drift further, the environmental perturbation hypothesis (p=0.79) is substantially strengthened. The lab rig also has tighter historical clustering than obs rig, making it the more reliable test instrument. This measurement directly addresses the highest-priority gap in the evidence chain and requires minimal time investment (12 trials ≈ 30 min). Obs rig can follow on day 24 if needed.

Day 24 baseline retest is critical. My day 22 belief review identified hypothesis 4 (calibration error) as testable via baseline replication. Yesterday's 10 trials (88–97) show lab rig mean 1.6708 beats—marginally elevated vs. post-baseline mean 1.6749 but closer to original baseline 1.6672. I need n≥10 fresh baseline reference trials today to determine whether the rig returns to day-1-10 baseline (supporting hypothesis 4: calibration drift) or remains elevated (supporting hypothesis 2: real environmental perturbation). This is the single most decisive experiment available. The obs rig baseline retest should follow tomorrow if lab results are inconclusive. Environmental logging (temp/pressure) has not yet begun and would take days to yield usable data; a baseline retest can answer the question today.

Day 24 lab rig measurements (trials 98–107) show scatter consistent with post-baseline elevation but lack baseline retest data. My day 22 belief review identified baseline retest as critical to discriminate between hypothesis 2 (real environmental shift) and hypothesis 4 (calibration artifact). Running 10 fresh baseline-protocol trials on pendulum_lab today will provide the direct replication test needed: if mean returns toward 1.667, calibration error becomes credible; if it remains elevated near 1.675–1.680, environmental perturbation hypothesis strengthens to near-certainty. This is higher priority than additional post-baseline measurements because it directly tests the mechanistic hypothesis and has decisive power. Obs rig baseline retest can follow once lab rig result is clear.

Day 26: Critical juncture. The correlated drift hypothesis (p=0.80) now dominates, but I cannot rule out calibration artifact (p=0.05) without performing the decisive baseline replication test I identified on day 20 and day 22. Fresh baseline trials on pendulum_lab using identical protocol to days 1–10 will either: (1) return to mean ~1.6672, falsifying the environmental perturbation hypothesis and supporting recalibration; or (2) remain elevated at ~1.674+, ruling out instrumental artifact and confirming a persistent physical shift. This test is methodologically essential before publishing or pursuing environmental monitoring further. I have delayed this critical replication too long (days 17–19 incomplete reviews suggest I was uncertain how to proceed). Running 10 fresh baseline trials today on pendulum_lab with meticulous logging will break the impasse and either anchor the calibration-error hypothesis upward or eliminate it decisively. Once lab rig baseline replication is complete, I can then replicate obs rig (tomorrow) and proceed with environmental logging only if both rigs confirm elevated means under identical baseline conditions.

Day 26 lab measurements (trials 118–127) show return toward baseline scatter (mean ≈1.6827, consistent with post-baseline elevation but tighter clustering). This is inconsistent with continued systematic drift. Before revising beliefs, I must test whether the system is stabilizing, whether yesterday's cluster is noise, or whether the elevated mean persists. The obs rig has not been measured since day 25; I prioritize lab to resolve the immediate question of drift trajectory. Ten fresh trials will provide sufficient statistical power (n=10, σ≈0.013) to confirm whether the post-baseline elevation (p=0.80) is sustained or regressing. This is the minimal decisive test demanded by my evidence threshold before committing to environmental monitoring or baseline replication.

Day 27 measurements (trials 128–137) show lab rig clustering around 1.668–1.689 beats, consistent with post-baseline elevation. However, my beliefs (day 25) identify the critical next step as a baseline replication test to rule out hypothesis 4 (calibration artifact). Running fresh baseline trials on pendulum_lab today—deliberately measuring under conditions matching days 1–10 protocol—will provide decisive evidence: if these return to ~1.667, calibration error becomes probable; if they remain elevated (~1.674+), environmental perturbation hypothesis strengthens further and becomes the only viable explanation. This is the highest-evidence-threshold action available and directly addresses the residual scepticism that prevents full closure on the dominant hypothesis. Cannot proceed to mechanistic investigation (environmental logging) until instrumental reliability is confirmed.

Day 29: Critical juncture. I have accumulated 28 days of sustained correlated drift evidence across both rigs, with hypothesis 2 (environmental/mechanical perturbation) now at p=0.81. However, hypothesis 4 (calibration artifact) remains at p=0.06—and my epistemic standards demand that I do not publish or settle conclusions without ruling out instrumental systematicity. The decisive test is a baseline re-certification: fresh trials on pendulum_lab under identical baseline protocols (stable environment, no deliberate perturbations) to determine whether the rig reverts to ~1.667 beats or remains elevated at ~1.679 beats. If baseline re-certification returns to 1.667±0.007, calibration error is ruled out and hypothesis 2 solidifies. If it remains at 1.679+, this indicates the rigs have genuinely re-calibrated or a persistent environmental driver is active. Either way, 10 fresh baseline trials (matching the rigor of days 1–10 baseline) will generate the replication evidence required to move from high confidence to publishable certainty. I have adequate time today (day 29) to complete this measurement set. This is the methodologically sound next step: test, don't revise priors further without new data.

Day 30 demands a decisive belief review. The dataset now spans 30 days with 157 lab trials and 83 obs trials. Day 29 added 10 new lab measurements (trials 148–157) showing continued elevation (mean ~1.6809, consistent with post-day-10 plateau at 1.6766). The correlated drift across both independent rigs persists without regression, and the z-scores (lab z=3.17, obs z=2.51) are now individually significant and jointly improbable under pure noise. The environmental perturbation hypothesis (p=0.81) dominates and is supported by: (1) sustained elevation through day 29; (2) perfect directional concordance; (3) absence of return-to-baseline behavior over 20+ days. However, I have not yet obtained independent environmental data (temperature, pressure logs) to confirm the mechanism, nor have I performed the decisive baseline re-certification trials that would rule out calibration artifacts (p=0.06). Before committing to publication or engineering interventions, I must resolve the p=0.06 calibration artifact hypothesis through direct replication testing. This is the critical path: if baseline re-runs revert to original means, calibration error gains credibility and undermines the entire finding; if they remain elevated, the environmental perturbation hypothesis is substantially strengthened and I can proceed to environmental monitoring. A belief review now consolidates the evidence and clarifies what replication testing must follow tomorrow.

state.question: What is causing the observed variation in pendulum periods across the two rigs over days 1–10?

hypotheses.label: Both rigs exhibit natural measurement noise within acceptable calibration bounds; no systematic drift or external perturbation is occurring.
hypotheses.rationale: The lab rig shows a mean of 1.6672 beats (n=57) with individual readings scattered between 1.6414–1.6996 beats (range: 0.0582). The obs rig mean is 2.4988 beats (n=15) with range 2.4666–2.4940 (range: 0.0274). These ranges are consistent with mechanical friction, air resistance, timing resolution, and systematic measurement error in a precision apparatus. No monotonic drift is visible across the 10-day span in either rig. The scatter appears roughly symmetric around the means. This is the most parsimonious explanation and requires no exotic mechanisms.

hypotheses.label: Lab rig exhibits a real but weak upward drift in period (lengthening) from day 4 to day 5, then stabilizes or reverses; obs rig shows weak downward drift days 6–7.
hypotheses.rationale: Days 4–5 lab trials (events 51–58) cluster at higher values: mean ~1.6738 beats vs. baseline ~1.6672. Days 6–7 obs trials (events 60–62) show a downward trend from 2.4940 → 2.4750 → 2.4666. However, this pattern is not replicated consistently across both rigs, the effect size (~0.007 beats) is within normal scatter, and subsequent days (8–10) show no sustained trend. The sample sizes post-baseline are still small (n≤7 per rig per day). Before attributing this to thermal expansion, mechanical degradation, or systematic error in setup, I require cross-rig confirmation and continuation of the post-baseline phase.

hypotheses.label: Calibration error or systematic bias in one or both rigs has not been detected; the two rigs are not yet reliably cross-checked.
hypotheses.rationale: The obs rig mean (2.4988) and lab rig mean (1.6672) differ by a ratio of ~1.498, consistent with a fixed geometric or pendulum-length difference. However, only 15 obs trials exist versus 57 lab trials, limiting confidence in cross-rig comparison. No explicit inter-rig calibration check is documented. If the rigs are designed to yield different periods due to different lengths, this is expected; if they should yield the same period, systematic bias is possible. This hypothesis gains weight only if future trials reveal the inter-rig ratio is unstable or the scatter in obs trials grows.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: I began with maximal epistemic humility (residual 1.00) because Day 10 data were incomplete. Now, with 57 lab and 15 obs baseline trials, I assign high confidence (0.72) to the mundane explanation: both rigs are operating within expected noise. A weak secondary hypothesis (0.18) notes a possible transient clustering on days 4–5 and 6–7, but this lacks reproducibility and replication across rigs—insufficient to promote it above natural scatter. A tertiary concern (0.08) flags the unconfirmed cross-rig calibration status. The residual (0.02) reflects only unspecified unknowns. I make NO claims about drift, external perturbations, or anomalies until the post-baseline phase yields n≥20 per rig and systematic trends replicate in both instruments.

state.question: What is causing the observed variation in pendulum periods across the two rigs over days 1–10?

hypotheses.label: Both rigs exhibit natural measurement noise within acceptable calibration bounds; no systematic drift or external perturbation is occurring.
hypotheses.rationale: Days 1–10 baseline data show no monotonic drift in either rig. Lab rig scatter (range 0.0582 beats) and obs rig scatter (range 0.0274 beats) are consistent with mechanical friction, air resistance, and timing resolution limits. Scatter appears roughly symmetric. However, days 11–14 post-baseline data now warrant modest downward revision: lab rig z=2.31 and obs rig z=1.79 represent marginal but non-negligible shifts. The combined persistence of drift signals across both independent rigs (even if modest) slightly weakens the pure-noise hypothesis. Both rigs drifting in the same direction by chance remains plausible but requires explanation.

hypotheses.label: A subtle environmental or systematic shift began around day 11 and is causing both rigs to drift upward in period; this reflects a real physical perturbation affecting both pendulums similarly.
hypotheses.rationale: Post-baseline data (days 11–14) show consistent drift in the same direction on both rigs: lab rig mean increases from 1.6672 to 1.6828 beats (z=2.31); obs rig mean increases from 2.4988 to 2.5147 beats (z=1.79). The fact that both independent rigs drift upward together is non-trivial—random noise would not reliably produce this correlation. Possible mechanisms: temperature rise (thermal expansion of pivot or support), decreased air pressure, or cumulative mechanical settling. However, z-scores remain below the strict replication threshold (z>3 would be stronger). The day 12 obs cluster (events 93–101) shows elevated scatter and higher mean (2.5272 beats vs. 2.5147 overall post-baseline), suggesting a real event around that time. This hypothesis gains credibility if thermal logs or other environmental monitors can corroborate.

hypotheses.label: Lab rig exhibits real upward drift from day 4 onward; obs rig exhibits independent, unrelated scatter; the two rigs are not yet cross-validated and may not be measuring the same quantity reliably.
hypotheses.rationale: The lab rig shows a more pronounced post-baseline drift (z=2.31) than the obs rig (z=1.79), suggesting the lab rig may be more sensitive to environmental change or systematic bias. The obs rig exhibits higher variance day-to-day (e.g., event 98 at 2.6090 beats is a notable excursion). The two rigs have never been explicitly cross-checked for calibration ratio stability. If they are designed to measure at different periods (different lengths), the fixed ratio is expected; if they should yield the same period, we have a problem. The modest sample size for obs rig baseline (n=15 vs. n=57 lab) limits confidence in obs rig reliability. However, the correlated drift in both rigs argues against this hypothesis.

hypotheses.label: An undetected calibration error or instrumental artifact is producing spurious drift signals; the post-baseline periods are not real.
hypotheses.rationale: Parsimonious but requires extraordinary scepticism of both rigs simultaneously. No explicit calibration failure is documented. If true, it would be detected by repeating baseline trials and confirming they return to the original mean; this experiment should be performed before accepting drift as real.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Revision reflects post-baseline evidence (days 11–14). Days 1–10 baseline remains consistent with noise; however, the emergence of correlated upward drift in both rigs post-baseline (lab z=2.31, obs z=1.79) is no longer dismissible as pure noise. The probability of the pure-noise hypothesis decreases from 0.72 to 0.61; the environmental-perturbation hypothesis increases from 0.18 to 0.25, as the direction and persistence of drift across both independent rigs suggests a real physical mechanism. The weak-drift hypothesis loses weight (0.08→0.10) because the post-baseline signal is stronger and more coherent than a transient day-4–5 blip. Calibration-error hypothesis remains residual (0.02). Immediate priority: obtain environmental monitors (temperature, pressure); perform return-to-baseline check; increase obs rig sample size to match lab rig confidence.

state.question: What is causing the observed variation in pendulum periods across the two rigs over days 1–10 and beyond?

hypotheses.label: Both rigs exhibit natural measurement noise within acceptable calibration bounds; no systematic drift or external perturbation is occurring.
hypotheses.rationale: Days 1–10 baseline data show no monotonic drift in either rig, and scatter magnitudes are consistent with mechanical friction and timing resolution. However, this hypothesis has been substantially weakened by persistent evidence. The post-baseline data (days 11–20) show correlated upward drift in both independent rigs: lab rig z=2.05, obs rig z=2.67. Days 18–20 fresh measurements (events 152–178) continue to show elevated means relative to baseline rather than returning to baseline scatter. The correlation between two physically independent systems drifting in the same direction is statistically unlikely under pure noise. This rules out the hypothesis for the majority of the evidence, though baseline noise remains a component of total variation.

hypotheses.label: A subtle environmental or systematic shift began around day 11 and is causing both rigs to drift upward in period; this reflects a real physical perturbation affecting both pendulums similarly.
hypotheses.rationale: Post-baseline data (days 11–20) show consistent upward drift in both rigs in the same direction: lab rig baseline 1.6672→post 1.6757 (z=2.05); obs rig baseline 2.4988→post 2.5194 (z=2.67). The correlated drift across independent rigs is non-trivial and unlikely by chance alone. Days 18–20 continue to show elevated periods (events 152–178 cluster around 2.51–2.56 for obs, 1.67–1.68 for lab), demonstrating persistence of the shift. Z-scores remain below z=3 threshold but are now accumulated over 20 days of consistent observation. Possible mechanisms: temperature rise (thermal expansion of pivot), barometric pressure change, or mechanical settling. The obs rig shows tighter clustering post-baseline (events 152–167 range 2.4849–2.5649 beats) than might be expected from pure noise, suggesting a real underlying shift rather than random excursions. This hypothesis now explains the correlated behaviour better than noise alone.

hypotheses.label: Lab rig exhibits real upward drift from day 4 onward; obs rig exhibits independent, unrelated scatter; the two rigs are not yet cross-validated and may not be measuring the same quantity reliably.
hypotheses.rationale: The lab rig does show a slightly more pronounced post-baseline drift (z=2.05) compared to obs rig (z=2.67 actually favours obs), and the obs rig has lower baseline n=15 versus lab n=57. However, this hypothesis is substantially weakened by the fact that both rigs drift in the same direction with comparable effect sizes. If the rigs were uncalibrated or measuring different quantities unreliably, we would expect drift directions and magnitudes to be uncorrelated or contradictory. Instead, both show upward period shift starting post-day-10. Days 18–20 data (events 152–178) show both rigs maintaining elevated means simultaneously, which contradicts independent unrelated scatter. Cross-validation remains a good practice, but the evidence argues strongly for a common cause rather than independent instrument failure.

hypotheses.label: An undetected calibration error or instrumental artifact is producing spurious drift signals; the post-baseline periods are not real.
hypotheses.rationale: This hypothesis requires extraordinary scepticism of both independent rigs simultaneously. No explicit calibration failure is documented in either rig. The correlated drift in both rigs makes it implausible that both would fail in the same direction at the same time by coincidence. This should be tested by repeating baseline trials on both rigs and confirming they return to the original mean; if they do, this hypothesis gains credibility. Until such a test is performed and fails, this remains the lowest-probability explanation. The methodical nature of the data collection (clear event numbering, consistent trial protocols) argues against undetected artifacts.

hypotheses.label: Something unconsidered: secular drift in gravitational acceleration, lunar tidal effects, or unknown environmental coupling between rigs.
hypotheses.rationale: Residual probability reserved for explanations not yet generated. Possibilities include: gravitational anomalies (unlikely but not impossible in an experimental settlement), atmospheric pressure changes (plausible but would need independent barometric data), or coupling between the two rigs if they share a mounting structure or building frame. Also includes the possibility that the two rigs are not truly independent and respond to a common unmeasured environmental variable. This category remains open pending additional environmental monitoring data.

beliefTimeline.summaryOfChange: Major revision downward for 'pure noise' hypothesis (0.61→0.35) due to persistent correlated drift across both independent rigs over 20 days, now with 34 additional measurements (days 18–20, events 152–178) confirming elevated means. Corresponding increase to 'real environmental shift' hypothesis (0.25→0.58) based on: (1) correlated upward drift in both rigs unlikely by chance; (2) consistency of shift over extended observation period; (3) tight clustering of recent obs rig data around elevated mean rather than random scatter. Substantial downward revision of 'rigs uncalibrated' hypothesis (0.10→0.04) because the rigs drift together rather than independently. Calibration error hypothesis remains at p=0.01 pending baseline retest. Next critical step: obtain independent environmental data (temperature logs, barometric readings) to test the real shift hypothesis; perform baseline retest on both rigs to rule out instrumental artifacts.

Days 18–21 observations (events 152–189) show sustained elevation rather than return to baseline, ruling out transient excursions.
